item.title: Nas-Backed Sweet Chick Shuts Down All Restaurants
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nas' ties to Sweet Chick stretch back more than a decade as the once-expanding restaurant chain announces its closure.
item.content:encoded:
Nas-backed Sweet Chick is shutting down all its restaurants, ending the chicken-and-waffles business that brought his Queens roots into dining rooms across New York.

The restaurant announced the closures Thursday in a social media statement. Its message thanked customers for their support without identifying a reason for the shutdown.

“After 14 years in business, we’ve made the difficult decision to close all Sweet Chick locations,” the company wrote.

Sweet Chick began in Williamsburg in 2013 before adding restaurants in the Lower East Side, Long Island City, Prospect Heights and Union Square.

Nas joined founder John Seymour’s expansion effort in 2015, when the business was looking beyond its first Brooklyn and Manhattan dining rooms.

For Nas, the Queens opening carried a family connection.

The Long Island City restaurant honored his father, jazz musician Olu Dara, with a hidden back room inspired by Harlem jazz clubs. Nas and Seymour celebrated that opening with relatives, friends and fellow rappers in April 2018.

Seymour described the partnership’s beginnings in an interview with Hypebeast. He had met Joey Bada$$ while opening the original Brooklyn restaurant and later crossed paths with him at SXSW.

Nas arrived as Seymour was discussing the possibility of bringing him into the business.

“We just talked about what we do as a brand, creating a community, building on culture,” Seymour recalled.

Their plans eventually included a different way of serving customers. In 2022, Sweet Chick announced Series A funding from Founders Table Restaurant Group, the company behind Chopt and Dos Toros.

The money was intended to support expansion and finish converting the restaurants to a fast-casual format.

That announcement described Nas as an early investor, while Seymour remained the founder leading the restaurant concept.

The financing came after Sweet Chick had already taken its food and music connections beyond New York, including a Los Angeles location.

Seymour had started changing the service model during the pandemic, according to the company’s announcement, before seeking money for additional restaurant openings.

The brand also collaborated with Clarks Originals on two Wallabee designs, translating its signature meal into caramel waffle and fried-chicken-inspired colors.

item.title: Chris Brown Agrees To $12,000 A Month In Temporary Child Support
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chris Brown and Diamond Brown reach an interim child support deal that raises his monthly payment while settlement talks continue.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Brown agreed to $12,000 in monthly child support, $25,000 in arrears and a $55,000 legal-fee advance to ex, Diamond Brown, TMZ reported.

The payment amount is temporary as the two sides continue settlement talks. Brown will also continue providing existing noncash support.

The agreement follows months of filings in Los Angeles about what Chris earns, which records Diamond Brown can see and how much he should contribute.

Diamond had proposed roughly $45,000 a month in October. Her request included household costs and expenses she wanted Chris to cover directly.

A later filing put her request at a minimum of $30,000 and her existing voluntary support at about $7,000.

That fight over the monthly amount led to a dispute over access to financial records. Diamond sought information from Chris Brown’s business managers to assess his earnings.

Earlier this month, the sides agreed to a protective order that limited how they could use any material produced.

“In no event shall the Confidential Materials be made public,” the order states. Diamond agreed not to review the protected papers herself while the two sides tried mediation.

Her lawyers could still review material within the order’s limits, and certain accounting records required additional clearance before she could see them.

The protective order left Chris Brown’s objections to the records requests unresolved.

If mediation didn’t settle child support or legal fees, their attorneys were to discuss whether Diamond should be allowed to see the documents.

That conversation was separate from the dispute over custody. Diamond’s records requests date to June 10, and Chris’s objections were filed August 14.

Under the confidentiality agreement, any protected documents used by the lawyers or their experts had to stay within the case, even if they could be useful in other disputes.

In earlier filings, Diamond sought primary physical custody while Chris asked for joint legal and physical custody. He also objected to paying all the legal expenses she sought then. Both sides had filed competing requests by June.

The prior order requires protected records to be returned or destroyed within 60 days after the case and any appeal conclude.

item.title: Bruno Mars Mourns Father Peter Hernandez, The Man Who Put Him Onstage
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Bruno Mars remembers his father, Peter Hernandez, the doo-wop bandleader who first put him onstage in Waikiki, Hawaii.
item.content:encoded:
Bruno Mars announced Thursday that his father, Peter Hernandez, had died at 74.

The singer shared family photos and remembered the man who put him onstage before he was old enough to start school.

Mars said in his tribute that he had hugged his father for the last time the week before.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time. If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music. He raised my four beautiful sisters, my brother, and me. In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again,” Bruno Mars said.

Hernandez shared his given name with his son, but he had his own history in music.

He grew up in New York, where he tagged along to his father’s gigs and fell for the sound of doo-wop. He moved to Hawaii at 25 and put together the Love Notes, an act that grew to 18 performers onstage.

Hernandez and Mars’ mother, Bernadette, worked the showrooms around Waikiki Beach. Mars joined them as Little Elvis and spent years performing the act.

He even played a young Elvis impersonator in the film Honeymoon in Vegas. His father told Hawaii News Now that he would wake at night and find his son still working on the moves he had seen on tape.

The band broke up after Mars’ parents split. He and his brother went to live with their father, and the three spent more than two years in a one-room building at a closed bird park. When Mars took 60 Minutes back there, he remembered how his dad kept finding places for them to stay.

Mars left Hawaii after high school, but he and his father still found their way back to the same stage.

The Love Notes opened for him in Honolulu, and at a show in Puerto Rico, Mars brought his father out and told the crowd who had taught him everything he knew.

Hernandez told Hawaii’s MidWeek that he and his son stayed in touch by phone and text when they weren’t together.

Music stayed in the family too, with Bruno’s brother Eric playing drums on tour and their four sisters performing together as The LYLAS. Mars later credited Black music, including doo-wop and R&B, with shaping his sound.

Mars closed the tribute with a message for Hernandez and Bernadette, who died in 2013: “I love you, Pops. Kiss Mom up there for me.”

item.title: Busta Rhymes Tells Veteran Rappers To Evolve Or Sit Down
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Busta Rhymes tells veteran rappers to keep evolving as he looks back on The Coming and his latest work with J Dilla's beats.
item.content:encoded:
Busta Rhymes thinks some veteran rappers “do need to sit down,” and not because they’ve reached a certain age.

He said on Apple Music’s Rap Life Review that the problem is getting comfortable enough to stop changing.

“Because they get stuck and they’re not evolving,” Busta said, explaining why he thinks some older MCs should step aside. “They’re a little too stubborn with ‘yesterday.'”

He brought that point of view to an episode looking back on 30 years of his debut and discussing his latest J Dilla project.

Busta had already made an impression as a member of Leaders of the New School and on records such as A Tribe Called Quest’s “Oh My God” and “The Scenario” before he made his solo debut.

When Elektra released The Coming in 1996, listeners got both the shouted hook of “Woo Hah!! Got You All in Check” and a much smoother turn on “It’s a Party.”

J Dilla was part of the production team The Ummah, which worked on the debut. The album’s 25th anniversary edition also includes his remix of “Woo Hah!!” and The Ummah’s remix of “It’s a Party.”

Their relationship continued across Busta’s solo catalog. After Dilla died in 2006, Busta used the Detroit producer’s beats to make the first Dillagence mixtape, which came out the following year.

Nearly two decades later, Busta went back to unreleased Dilla beats for Dillagence II. The project started after a call from Dilla’s mother, Ma Dukes, who wanted to mark 20 years since her son’s death.

Busta said he first planned to make one song before the idea grew into an album. The 19-track release arrived in August and pairs the late producer’s work with a D’Angelo vocal on “This Woman.” Busta and Dilla share the artist credit on the album.

Using an old beat doesn’t mean Busta approaches it the same way every time. In a separate interview on the Zach Sang Show, he said the way Dilla built a track left room for choices other than the rapid-fire rapping many fans associate with him.

“I’ve never speed rapped on a Dilla beat because his music doesn’t warrant that,” Busta said.

item.title: Eminem Stalking Defendant Claimed He Was Her Child’s Father, Prosecutor Says
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A prosecutor says Nicole Savage claimed Eminem fathered her child. A Michigan judge has ordered a competency evaluation.
item.content:encoded:
A woman charged with stalking Eminem told people at his Michigan property that the rapper was her child’s father, prosecutors allege.

A judge has ordered a competency evaluation for Nicole Gwen Savage, who is accused of going to the home despite an order barring contact.

Assistant Macomb County Prosecutor Steve Fox described her remarks in the motion requesting the exam,

The Detroit News reported. Fox wrote that Savage also claimed to be a Russian operative and said Vladimir Putin was her father.

The prosecution cited the remarks in its request for an evaluation.

In Michigan, a competency exam looks at whether defendants understand the proceedings and can help their attorneys prepare a defense. The examiner sends a report to the court, and both sides can present evidence before the judge decides whether the case can proceed.

Savage, 46, of Trenton, Michigan, was charged with aggravated stalking after an encounter at a home Eminem owns in Clinton Township on October 27. According to the Macomb County Prosecutor’s Office, an order was already in place barring her from contacting him.

The rapper’s security staff called police, and officers took Savage into custody without incident.

“Everyone deserves to feel safe in their own home and go about their daily lives without fear of being harassed or stalked,” Macomb County Prosecutor Peter J. Lucido said when his office announced the charge.

Magistrate Ryan Zemke arraigned Savage in the 41B District Court on Oct. 28. Aggravated stalking carries a maximum five-year prison sentence in Michigan, according to county prosecutors. They described it as the most serious charge the evidence supported at the time.

Zemke set bond at $250,000, payable in cash or through a surety, without the option of posting 10 percent.

He ordered Savage not to contact Eminem, possess weapons or leave Michigan. She would have to wear a GPS monitor if released on bond.

Eminem was the subject of a separate stalking case that ended in a prison sentence in June 2025.

A Macomb County jury convicted Matthew David Hughes of first-degree home invasion and aggravated stalking after Hughes entered the rapper’s property in August 2024.

Hughes must serve at least 18 years before he can seek parole.

item.title: Freddie Gibbs & The Alchemist Reunite Inside GTA VI’s The Safe Trap
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Freddie Gibbs and The Alchemist lend their voices to The Safe Trap, a GTA VI podcast from the series that gave them Fetti.
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Gibbs and The Alchemist voice characters together in Grand Theft Auto VI. The Alfredo collaborators appear in The Safe Trap, an in-game podcast from the franchise where they recorded the song that inspired their Alfredo title.

Rockstar’s official credits identify Gibbs as the voice of “Freddie” and The Alchemist as the voice of “The Alchemist.” The two longtime collaborators appear together in the cast listing for the in-game show.

Rockstar also credits Shaundrea Tijera DeWitt as Reena and William Engram, who performs as Poondaga, as Donny DuLo.

A Pro-Gamer guide lists The Safe Trap among the game’s on-demand programs, alongside other episodic shows. Rockstar’s overview says the game lets players listen on demand in vehicles or on foot with headphones or earbuds.

Their relationship with Rockstar stretches back well before this launch. The Alchemist and Oh No built Welcome to Los Santos around the world of Grand Theft Auto V, with Gibbs among its guest artists.

Rockstar’s announcement for that project highlighted “Fetti,” the Gibbs and Curren$y collaboration. The music also appeared on The Lab, an in-game station hosted by Alchemist and Oh No under their radio identities, the Chemical Bro and Dr No.

Rockstar also brought Alchemist, Oh No and Wavves together for a GTA Online session discussing their soundtrack work.

That earlier game left a mark on the duo’s work away from Rockstar. “We came up with the name Alfredo years ago when we recorded the song ‘Fetti’ for GTA V,” Gibbs’ manager Ben “Lambo” Lambert told Hypebeast.

Outside gaming, their partnership produced Alfredo in 2020 and its sequel in 2025. The first album earned a Grammy nomination for Best Rap Album, according to Gibbs’ official Warner Records biography.

They also took the collaboration into film. As AllHipHop previously reported, both starred in Alfredo: The Movie, a Tokyo-set crime short released alongside the single “1995” during the second album’s rollout.

The film used Japanese dialogue with English subtitles. It brought the pair together as performers in front of the camera before their latest speaking roles.

Gibbs’ acting résumé also includes Down With the King, Power Book IV: Force and Bust Down.

item.title: Snoop Dogg Gives $100K To D.O.C.’s School To Teach Texas Teens How To Build Video Games
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Snoop Dogg puts six figures behind The D.O.C.'s free North Texas program, which gives teens a start in game design.
item.content:encoded:
Snoop Dogg put $100,000 behind a free North Texas program that teaches middle and high school students how to build video games.

The gift gives The D.O.C.’s nonprofit a third of what it hopes to raise by year-end.

The D.O.C. founded DOC CARES, which runs Dreams Experience Academy for students in grades seven through 12. In its announcement, the nonprofit put the cost of supporting one student for a term at $2,500.

“Too many young people grow up shaping culture without ever being shown the economic opportunities available to them. Snoop and I know this better than most. Snoop’s gift and our Finish Strong initiative will help us reach more students, in North Texas and beyond, with the skills, access and belief to see themselves not only participating in industries that shape culture, but eventually leading and owning within them,” The D.O.C. said.

The academy starts with game design, giving students a chance to build something they can show to people who work in the field.

The Dallas pilot, held with For Oak Cliff and the Moorland Family YMCA, put students to work researching who might play their games and building prototypes. They pitched the results to a panel, then the academy took the program to three more North Texas schools, including St. Philip’s and two Texans Can Academies campuses.

Snoop’s role in the program predates the gift. He was among the contributors to the pilot alongside Dr. Dre and Erykah Badu. The first round of students also met people from Marvel and the Dallas Mavericks.

DOC CARES founding president Chris Gannett said the gift would help the nonprofit expand in 2027. The group is also developing instruction in music, content creation and applied artificial intelligence.

“Snoop’s gift gives us real momentum heading into year-end, and every additional donation helps us serve more students while building toward a much larger footprint in 2027,” Gannett said.

When The D.O.C. and Gannett unveiled the academy at Dallas’ Kessler Theater, Badu took part in the launch.

By then, The D.O.C. had already spent years working in music, writing for artists including Dr. Dre and mentoring Snoop.

The D.O.C. first previewed the fundraising drive in Las Vegas when the Paid In Full Foundation presented him with its Grandmaster honor.

item.title: Doe Boy Skips The Major Streamers To Give Away His New Mixtape
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Doe Boy takes his case for mixtapes off the timeline and puts a free download in listeners' hands through the Untitled app.
item.content:encoded:
Doe Boy gave away Mixtape Beezy through the Untitled app after arguing that the biggest streaming services leave new rappers without the kind of attention mixtape sites once gave them. The Cleveland rapper used his own release to show what he wanted to see more of: a full tape people could get for free.

“FREE DOWNLOAD. EXCLUSIVELY ON THE UNTITLED APP,” he wrote in his release announcement on X. The post paired the project title with a direct link to Untitled, giving listeners a route to the tape alongside his call to bring mixtapes back.

The release followed several days of Doe Boy making the case for the sites that helped artists get heard before they had a hit. He pointed to LiveMixtapes and Spinrilla, where people could find whole projects from rappers they might not have heard anywhere else.

“Mixtape platforms used to make Superstars,” he wrote on X. He argued that today’s leading rappers rose through those sites, writing that the “biggest in the game blew up off Livemixtapes, Spinrilla, etc.”

He also acknowledged that YouTube and SoundCloud helped artists break, rather than crediting mixtape sites alone.

Doe Boy knows how far a tape can travel. In an interview with Its Up There Podcast, he recalled Future finding his music through his True Story mixtape and talked about the phone call that followed. The relationship put the Cleveland rapper in the Freebandz orbit.

Years later, he and DJ Esco put out 56 Birdz through Freebandz and Epic Records. Epic announced the 2020 project as their first full-length collaboration, following Esco’s work with Future on 56 Nights.

The latest move comes as other artists are questioning how listeners find new music. Meek Mill recently made the case for artists to build their own platforms instead of leaving those decisions to streaming services and record labels.

He took the argument further by calling for an awards show run by artists.

Doe Boy’s earlier 56 Birdz collaboration with Esco arrived on the fifth anniversary of 56 Nights, the Future mixtape that helped establish the producer’s reputation beyond his work as a touring DJ.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: R. Kelly Judge Strikes Nine Filings She Links To Aaron Mazie
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: A Chicago judge tosses nine filings in R. Kelly's criminal case after an appeals court warned Aaron Mazie about filing for others.
item.content:encoded:
R. Kelly‘s Chicago criminal case drew nine filings from someone a federal judge identified as their apparent author: Aaron Corbin Mazie. U.S. District Judge Martha Pacold struck all nine on November 17, citing an earlier warning from the appeals court that Mazie could not ask for relief on someone else’s behalf.

Pacold described the submissions as filings “that appear to be by Aaron Mazie” in the one-page order reviewed by AllHipHop. She gave another reason for striking them: “Additionally, none of the filings state a cognizable claim to relief.” In other words, the court found no legally recognized basis for granting what the papers sought.

The order deals with nine docket entries in the Chicago prosecution. Pacold did not identify Mazie as Kelly’s lawyer or make a definitive finding that he wrote each document. Her decision to strike the filings leaves the singer’s sentence in place.

Mazie had already gone to the Seventh Circuit himself. He filed a petition seeking an extraordinary court order in June 2025 and asked to participate as a friend of the court. The appeals court denied the petition in July and later declined to rehear it. A motion seeking immediate release and reparations in that same proceeding was filed without further action in November 2025.

Mazie tried again in December 2025. The Seventh Circuit denied that petition and related motions on December 17. The appeals court’s warning was specific: “Petitioner Aaron Mazie may not seek relief on behalf of another person.” It also cautioned that further filings advocating for other people could bring sanctions.

Kelly was convicted in Chicago in 2022 on three counts of producing child sexual abuse material and three counts of enticing minors to engage in sexual activity. He received a 20-year sentence in that case in 2023. Nineteen years run alongside his 30-year New York sentence; one year runs after it.

Kelly’s own attorneys took a separate route in July, filing a formal clemency request with the Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney.

In another case in June 2026, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims required Mazie to obtain its chief judge’s permission before filing a new case there on his own.

item.title: Rihanna Reunites With Her “We Found Love” Director For Dior Campaign With Rocki
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Rihanna and her daughter Rocki star in Lady Dior 2027, directed by her 'We Found Love' collaborator and scored by Fela Kuti.
item.content:encoded:
Rihanna brought her daughter Rocki into Dior’s new handbag campaign and teamed up again with the director behind some of her biggest music videos. Melina Matsoukas directed the film for Lady Dior 2027, which puts Rihanna and Rocki on screen together to Fela Kuti’s “Lady.”

Dior released the campaign Thursday, with photographs by Sam Rock and creative direction by Jonathan Anderson.

The pictures show Rihanna alone and with Rocki, her third child with A$AP Rocky. Dior credits Benjamin Bruno for styling and Jahleel Weaver as Rihanna’s stylist. In one photograph, mother and daughter wear black leather jackets, with a pale pink quilted bag in the foreground.

“A lady is a prism. In a way that light shines through a prism and becomes multidimensional, and every color performs at a different angle,” Rihanna said in a statement.

Matsoukas and Rihanna were already regular collaborators by the time they made “We Found Love” in 2011.

The director had worked with her on “Hard” and “Rude Boy.” For “We Found Love,” Matsoukas cast boxer Dudley O’Shaughnessy opposite Rihanna and shot their turbulent romance in Belfast.

“I would set something up and they would just take it way further,” she said in an interview about what Rihanna and O’Shaughnessy improvised.

The video won MTV’s Video of the Year and a Grammy for Best Short Form Music Video. For the Dior film, Matsoukas worked with a record made decades before that collaboration.

“Lady” comes from Kuti’s 1972 album Shakara. Dior credited Partisan Records and BMG Rights Management in the film’s music licensing.

Dior has worked with Rihanna on campaigns for more than a decade. Steven Klein shot her 2015 Secret Garden campaign at Versailles and took her back to the palace for her debut as the face of J’adore in 2024.

Rihanna first introduced Rocki publicly last year with a photograph of herself holding her newborn and a second image of tiny pink boxing gloves.

Thursday’s campaign puts them together again, this time in front of Matsoukas’ camera.
